newsitem.title: UK: Labour morale high ahead of crucial UK by-election.
newsitem.headline: Labour morale high ahead of crucial UK by-election.

text.p: If British Prime Minister John Major loses office at the next general election, his political tombstone may well read: mortally wounded in Wirral South.
British parliamentary by-elections are traditionally a chance for voters to give the government of the day a bloody nose. Seats lost in mid-term often swing back at the next national poll.
But Thursday's by-election in Wirral South, a prosperous corner of northwest England, looks like being different.

With three months at most before a general election, political analysts believe the outcome will be an important pointer to whether Major's Conservatives can win an unprecedented fifth straight term or will lose power for the first time since 1979 to Tony Blair's Labour party.
It does not take long touring this microcosm of middle England to find out why opinion polls are predicting Labour will romp home in what has always been a safe Conservative seat.

"We've had 18 years of the Conservatives and I just think it's time for a change," said Gordon Morris, 68, who used to work at Unilever, the largest local employer and one of the firms that makes the Wirral peninsular the home of the chemical industry.

"There's just something about Tony Blair -- he's just a bit more 'go' than John Major," said Morris, whose vote at the last election helped to re-elect Conservative Barry Porter with more than 50 percent of the vote. Porter died in November.

Conservative candidate Les Byrom, a former surveyor who now runs his own business, remains confident. "We're fighting for victory. This is traditional Tory territory and our job is to get the Conservative vote out on Thursday," he said.
But over lunch in the Wheatsheaf, a pub in the well-heeled village of Raby in the heart of the constituency, the scale of Byrom's task became apparent.

Byrom has brought Social Security Secretary Peter Lilley to open the 17th century pub's new conservatory, but David Dunn and his wife -- the sort of people who should be the bedrock of the ruling party's support -- are unimpressed.

"We like the prime minister, but I'm not too sure about the others," Dunn, 58, a retired bank manager, said. "We're voting for individuals in this by-election and I think we might go to Labour in this particular instance."
Polls suggest Labour, which has poured vast resources into Wirral South, also looks set to siphon off support from the centre-left Liberal Democrats, Britain's third-biggest party.
Barbara Morris, the wife of the Unilever pensioner who is thinking of switching to Labour, voted for the Liberal Democrats last time and has yet to make her mind up about Thursday.
She says the Conservatives will not get her vote, but nor will the Liberal Democrats: "I just don't think they have much chance of forming a majority."

Some 150 Labour members of parliament will have visited Wirral South by Thursday to support their candidate Ben Chapman, 56, a former senior civil servant in Blair's moderate mould who can be counted on not to rock the party boat.
Blair himself plans his third visit on the eve of the poll.
"We're not taking anything for granted," said Andrew Smith, Labour's transport spokesman. Despite the caution, Labour's morale is palpably higher than in the Conservative camp.

Labour knows that if it achieves the swing of more than eight percent it needs to overturn Porter's 8,183 majority it will gain a major psychological advantage going into the general election, widely expected to be held on May 1.
"This is a constituency that by its nature and inclination is a safe Tory seat, said Ian McCartney, a Labour employment spokesman who is heading the campaign.
"We're asking people to break the habit of a lifetime."
